🌎 BEYOND THE 956

Dolores Huerta, the civil rights and labor leader who co-founded the United Farm Workers and gave the movement its rallying cry, “Sí, se puede,” has died at 96.

Huerta died on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, at her home in Bakersfield, California, according to a statement from her family. Family spokesman Erik Olvera told The New York Times that the cause was cancer.

“We are deeply saddened to announce that our beloved mother, Dolores Huerta, has passed away today at the age of 96,” her family wrote in a statement shared on her official Instagram account, asking for privacy as they mourn.

Born Dolores Clara Fernández on April 10, 1930, in Dawson, New Mexico, and raised in Stockton, California, Huerta began her working life as a teacher before turning to community organizing on behalf of farmworkers.

In 1962, she co-founded the National Farm Workers Association with Cesar Chavez, the organization that later became the United Farm Workers. She helped lead the historic Delano grape strike and the nationwide grape boycott that brought the conditions of California farmworkers to national attention, and the movement's campaigns helped lead to the California Agricultural Labor Relations Act of 1975, which established collective bargaining rights for farmworkers.

Huerta became widely known for the phrase “Sí, se puede” — “Yes, we can” — which grew from the farmworker movement into a rallying cry for labor and civil rights movements far beyond California's fields.

Her work earned her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, presented by President Barack Obama in 2012. She went on to found the Bakersfield-based Dolores Huerta Foundation in 2002, and she kept marching, speaking and organizing well into her 90s, advocating for women's rights, immigration reform and greater political representation for Latino communities.

Sources: The New York Times (family spokesman Erik Olvera); Associated Press; Reuters; family statement via the Dolores Huerta Foundation.
